question: In a recent answer, the Commission stated that the accession of the European Union to the European Convention on Human Rights was a priority for the Commission1. It would seem, however, that European Court of Human Rights is experiencing impartiality problems, to which civil society organisations draw attention on a regular basis. One such problem concerns the truthfulness and accuracy of judges’ CVs.

One judge allegedly improperly used the title of a regulated profession2, which is a criminal offence. In the context of the process of EU accession to the European Convention on Human Rights – which will involve participation in the appointment of judges – how will the Commission ensure that candidates’ CVs are thoroughly checked and verified?
answer: The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe elects the judges of the European Court of Human Rights. The election process consists of two phases. Firstly, there’s a national selection procedure where each High Contracting Party nominates three qualified candidates. The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe has adopted guidelines that states are expected to follow during this process (3).

Secondly, the Parliamentary Assembly conducts an election procedure. In this phase, a special parliamentary committee evaluates the qualifications of the three candidates and reviews the fairness of the national selection procedure. Only after this assessment does the Assembly proceed with the final election of one judge among the three candidates submitted by the High Contracting Party.

Accession to the Convention is a priority for the EU. In March 2023, negotiators from the EU and each Member State of the Council of Europe reached a provisional agreement on revised accession instruments (4).

These instruments stipulate that upon the EU’s accession to the Convention, a delegation of Members of the European Parliament will have the right to vote during the Parliamentary Assembly’s election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights. Additionally, the EU will have the opportunity to nominate a judge to the European Court of Human Rights.
The EU’s selection process for nominating its three candidates will have to be in line with the relevant guidelines established by the Committee of Ministers.
